title: A Door Left Open
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 20 of 40
content:
For three days after the apology, Snape left his office door open.

Not wide.

Never wide.

About six inches.

Enough that I could see lamplight from the classroom.

Enough that if I needed him, I did not have to knock on a closed barrier.

He did not mention it.

Neither did I.

We returned to ordinary work.

Ordinary, by then, meant arguing over aconite quality, drafting evidence summaries, practicing Patronus charms after dinner, and occasionally realizing we were standing too close.

My Patronus still refused to choose a recognizable form.

“Again,” Snape said.

Silver mist burst from my wand, gathered itself into something with legs, and collapsed.

I swore.

“Elegant.”

“You're not helping.”

“I am not responsible for your vocabulary.”

“You're responsible for half of it.”

His mouth twitched.

“Again.”

I tried.

This time the shape ran three steps before dissolving.

Snape's eyes brightened.

“There.”

“I saw.”

“Then stop looking surprised.”

“I am allowed to be pleased.”

“Privately.”

“Are you pleased?”

His expression went carefully blank.

I smiled.

“Thought so.”

We returned to the dungeon late.

The office door was open.

Snape entered first and did not close it behind him.

I sat at the classroom table with the evidence ledger while he sorted letters inside.

From my chair, I could see only part of him: a sleeve, the edge of his desk, the corner of the hidden door.

It felt strangely domestic.

Not romantic, exactly.

More intimate than that.

The comfort of knowing another person was nearby without needing their attention.

I had almost finished the ledger when Snape called, “Come here.”

I looked toward the doorway.

“Permission?”

A pause.

“Yes.”

I entered.

He had spread documents across the desk.

At the center was a letter from Harry Potter.

Snape looked offended by its existence.

“What does he want?” I asked.

“To testify.”

“I thought he already agreed.”

“He has now written eight paragraphs explaining why.”

“That sounds like Harry Potter.”

“You know him?”

“Only publicly.”

“Then do not defend him.”

I leaned over the letter.

The handwriting was messy and direct. I did not read the private details, only the lines Snape had marked.

Potter intended to state that Snape had protected him, served Dumbledore, sent the doe Patronus, and remained loyal to the mission at the cost of his reputation and life.

Snape had underlined reputation twice.

“You hate this,” I said.

“Yes.”

“Because it's wrong?”

“No.”

“Because it's Harry?”

“Partly.”

“Because he makes you sound heroic?”

Snape's mouth tightened.

“There was nothing heroic about many of my choices.”

“He doesn't say there was.”

“He will be heard as saying it.”

“People do like simple stories.”

“Yes.”

I pulled the second chair closer and sat.

“What do you want him to say?”

“The truth.”

“Which truth?”

His eyes narrowed.

I gestured to the letter.

“You've taught me better than that. Facts without context. Context without absolution. What do you want in the record?”

Snape looked down at his hands.

“That I joined willingly.”

I stayed quiet.

“That I served Voldemort before I turned.”

I nodded.

“That I passed on part of a prophecy without knowing whom it endangered, then cared who it endangered only when I learned Lily was a target.”

His voice was flat with practiced cruelty toward himself.

“That my first request to Dumbledore was for her life, not her husband's or child's.”

“Yes.”

His eyes flicked toward me, perhaps expecting interruption.

I gave none.

“That I bullied students. That I favored my own House. That I carried grudges into classrooms where they did not belong.”

I nodded again.

“And that you also spied for the Order for years,” I said when he stopped. “That you protected Harry. That you protected students under the Carrows. That you killed Dumbledore because he asked you to, not because Voldemort ordered you to.”

His face tightened.

“Yes.”

“Both.”

“Yes.”

I looked at Potter's letter.

“Then write back.”

“Absolutely not.”

“Coward.”

His head snapped up.

The word was dangerous with him.

I knew why.

I had used it anyway, lightly but not thoughtlessly.

His face went hard.

Then he saw my expression.

Not accusation.

Challenge.

A long silence.

“Manipulative,” he said.

“Effective.”

“Cheap.”

“Still effective.”

He took out a sheet of parchment.

I stood.

“I'll leave you to it.”

“Stay.”

The word stopped me.

Snape looked equally startled by it.

I sat again.

He wrote.

Slowly.

The letter was not sentimental.

Of course it wasn't.

He thanked Potter for offering testimony, then requested that the testimony include facts less flattering to him. He listed them with brutal clarity. He stated that service after defection did not erase service before it. He asked Potter not to repeat private memories beyond what was legally necessary.

Then he stopped.

“What?” I asked.

“Nothing.”

“My favorite word.”

His mouth tightened.

He wrote one final line.

I could not see it.

He folded the letter and sealed it.

“What did you add?”

“Private correspondence.”

“Fair.”

He looked at me.

“You are not going to ask?”

“I just did.”

“And accepted refusal.”

“I'm growing.”

“Disturbing.”

The sealed letter stayed on the desk while he straightened the rest of the paperwork. I kept thinking about the way he'd asked whether I intended to read it anyway.

"Can I ask a different question?" I said.

He looked up over his glasses. "You generally do."

"Do you want me here while you send it?"

His expression changed, just a little. "I had not considered that it was something I could request."

"You can request company without handing me the envelope."

He examined the wax seal. Whatever he'd written about the past was his to tell. I knew enough about the people involved to understand how dangerous a careless rumor could be, and not enough to decide the details for them.

"I'd like you to stay," he said.

"All right."

I sat with my notes while he recorded the recipient's address on a separate slip. He didn't show me the letter. I didn't pretend not to notice that he was trembling when he put it into the outgoing tray.

"Was it difficult?" I asked.

"Appallingly."

"Want me to tell you that you've done a good thing?"

"I should prefer you tell me whether the seal is intact."

"It is."

"Then we shall begin with that."

He found a second envelope for the school records and placed the private letter in the correct tray. It was not a ceremony, only an act of putting one piece of information where it belonged.

I leaned back in the chair. "For what it's worth, I like that you can say no to me."

"An unfortunate revelation."

"I'm ethically non-monogamous, and I prefer polyamory. Boundaries aren't a test of who loves someone best. They're part of how I know I can keep choosing a relationship."

He went quiet. Then he shifted the candle farther from the paper, an almost absurdly ordinary gesture.

"I understand the argument," he said. "I may even be persuaded by it."

I smiled. We sat together until the ink dried, and I went back to my own work without opening the letter or imagining that I had earned the right to.

We returned to the classroom.

Near midnight, I packed my notes.

Snape remained in the office.

The door was still open.

“Good night,” I called.

He appeared in the doorway.

“Good night.”

I took three steps.

“Wait.”

I turned.

He stood with one hand on the doorframe.

“I wrote that I remember his mother as herself,” he said.

I went still.

Not just Lily as Harry's mother.

Lily as herself.

“And?”

“That he should do the same.”

Something tightened behind my ribs.

“That was kind.”

His face immediately closed.

“Do not ruin it.”

“I wouldn't dream of it.”

He looked at me.

I looked back.

For a moment, neither of us moved.

Then he stepped aside from the doorway.

Not away.

Aside.

Making room.

“You may use the kettle,” he said.

I blinked.

“In the back room?”

“Yes.”

“Without asking?”

“Within reason.”

I smiled slowly.

“Careful.”

His eyes narrowed.

“That sounds dangerously like trust.”

“Go to bed.”

I laughed and left.

The open door did not remain open every night.

That would have made it a performance.

Sometimes I arrived and found it shut because Severus wanted quiet. Sometimes the ward flashed red because he was speaking with Minerva or reviewing testimony for the Ministry. Once I knocked and he simply called, “Not tonight.”

I went upstairs.

The next morning he stopped beside me at breakfast.

“You are not offended?”

“By a closed door?”

His expression said that yes, apparently this was a serious question.

“No.”

“You did not ask why.”

“You told me what you needed.”

He studied me with the wary concentration he normally reserved for unknown reagents.

“That is all?”

“That is all.”

He sat across from me.

Five minutes later, without explanation, he pushed the marmalade toward my side of the table because he had remembered I liked it.

I did not make a fuss.

The open door mattered because it was chosen.

So did the closed one.

By the end of the week, I understood that intimacy with Severus was not constant access. It was knowing a boundary would survive being used.

Behind me, he did not close the office door.

bridge_outro: A door left open mattered differently after I had seen the Lanternweald. At Moonroot Archive, a little door opened onto a reading room of books volunteered by people from worlds that disagreed about nearly everything. I found Toph testing the walls with one bare foot while Greg tried to decide whether a record player counted as a scholarly instrument. I laughed, unexpectedly, and thought of Severus making room in ways that would never look generous to anyone who had not learned his language. I did not mistake the archive's openness for permission to demand it of him. Trust was not the absence of doors. It was the right to close them, and the choice to open them again.
